candidate.answerReason: The figure starts with side lengths 1, 2, and 3 tiles. Thus the sixth and seventh squares contain 36 and 49 tiles, and their difference is 13.

methods.label: Count rows of tiles
methods.explanation:
The first three squares have side lengths of 1, 2, and 3 tiles. Since each new side is one tile longer, the sixth square has 6 rows of 6 tiles, and the seventh has 7 rows of 7 tiles. Their tile counts are therefore \(6\times6=36\) and \(7\times7=49\).

Subtracting gives the number of additional tiles:
\[
49-36=13.
\]
The seventh square requires \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: This uses elementary pattern continuation, multiplication, and subtraction.

methods.label: Count only the added tiles
methods.explanation:
The figure begins with a square one tile across, so the sixth square is 6 tiles across and the seventh is 7 tiles across.

Imagine keeping the sixth square in one corner of the seventh. Add a column of 6 tiles beside it, making a rectangle 6 tiles tall and 7 tiles wide. Then add a row of 7 tiles across the top. These two added pieces fill the larger square, and they do not overlap. Thus the number of new tiles is
\[
6+7=13.
\]
The answer is \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Counting a new row and column gives a complete elementary spatial argument without algebra.
